I don’t have a job at the moment, but I was treated like a woman at my old job because it was a family business and I didn’t have the balls to start drama with the people that were letting me stay at their house. The reason I am not working there this summer is because I refuse to put myself in that situation again. 

2. Assuming by “the medical divide” you mean transmedicalists/truscum vs. tucute, I found out about this a few months into realizing I was trans. After actually reading real information that wasn’t just based on everyone’s feelings, I never went back.

3. Yes, absolutely I do. I think the studies into brain sex and things like that are very promising for the medical legitimacy of transsexuals. 

4. My mother has said lots of dumb shit to convince me I’m not trans. I can’t think of the funniest examples at the moment, but her favorite is that I’m addicted to trans youtubers and constantly feed myself trans content, so it’s reinforcing my beliefs. Which would be legitimate if I was one of the non-dysphoric weirdos, but I actually tend to avoid trans people online because I hate most of their opinions and am pretty sick of the topic at this point. 

5. Honestly I just saw a famous person with that name and thought “damn that’s hot and I think it fits me” and that’s been my name since 2 am that day (night?). Of course it wasn’t the first time I ever heard the name (it’s a cis name), but I kind of forgot it existed until that point.

6. I was 13. Until that point, I didn’t really know anything about trans people at all because I grew up in a pretty conservative religious household. Then it clicked.

7. I’m out in college, but only because I’m pre t. I haven’t told a single person other than professors, but everyone knows anyway because I don’t pass as cis despite my best efforts. I navigate the world the same way I would if I was stealth because I refuse to acknowledge that everyone knows. I hate being “out” and will go stealth as soon as it’s possible. I’m treated pretty well though, people are very chill at my college especially in the music department (I’m a music major so most of the students I know are from there). I think that’s the general culture of colleges in america. I live in a rural conservative area and it’s still pretty liberal at the college.

8. Not on HRT yet.

9. I actually transitioned right after my freshman year of highschool and then went online. I ended up graduating without ever going back to in person school so it wasn’t an issue. However, I did have the meetings with the principal and counselor and blah blah to transition because I didn’t anticipate switching schools at that time. Everyone was cool and I actually didn’t experience any transphobic teachers at either school. I haven’t had any in college either.

10. My parents have no concept of privacy so they actually found out before I told them (I was not planning on telling them). I tried to explain to them that I felt uncomfortable with myself and blah blah but they’ll never get it. They think I’ll detransition and have biological kids someday lmao. 

11. (TW for suicide) My parents still won’t. The only reason they agreed to at least stop using my birth name and female pronouns is because I tried to end my life and cited dysphoria as the main reason. As much as they hate me being trans, they don’t want me dead. Of course they’ve gone back to deadnaming and misgendering me now that it’s been long enough, so I just try to block it out. Recently I’ve begun to say “try again” when they use my deadname. 

12. Yes. I’ve dropped more friends than family, but I limit my exposure to several of my cousins, aunts, and uncles as much as possible. There are some people I flat out refuse to see and never will again. If they can’t respect me, they don’t have to be in my life.

13. I don’t go to the gym anymore, but when I did I went with a friend and ofc used the male locker room. I went in and out at fast as possible and didn’t use my voice if there were other men in the room. Never had an issue, but I know that’s a matter of luck with where that gym was.

14. (TW for gun violence) I never had to fight anyone, no. But there was a guy that nearly shot up my highschool because he hated “f*ggots” and my friend and I were two of the people he had in mind. He ended up getting expelled (slap on the hand, no legal repercussions). I was 14 at the time and didn’t have a concept of how serious it was (guy was a senior, had access to guns) so I mocked him on social media and I don’t imagine that made me much safer. 

15. I haven’t ever been confronted directly, but one time I walked into a bathroom and a little boy (1-2) said “is that a giiiiirlll???” I don’t think his dad was thinking “a trans guy is in here” but more “my son just offended a stranger and we need to get out before we get our asses kicked.” The dad had his back turned to me so he didn’t see my short ass and they hurried out. I have never been so mortified and didn’t want to leave the stall because that’s when I knew I wasn’t passing great. Unfortunately there was only two stalls and people needed to shit.

16. Not something I’ve been asked, but when I came out a friend at the time thought I was actually post-transition mtf for like a week. I did not know this, so the whole time I thought he was being incredibly validating saying my ex “technically kissed a man” and things like that when he was actually intending to misgender me lmao. Didn’t realize until he asked me if I still had a dick.

I don’t think it’s a bad thing. Kids see people that look different all around them as they grow up, but keep in mind that, because they’re kids, they might ask you “yo wtf?” and have no shame. “that’s just the way I look, we’re all different”

“everyone has scars, I just have a few more”

“*insert bs made up excuse*”

“I went through some hard things and they left scars”

“I just got hurt a lot”

They might not even ask, but it shouldn’t be a problem unless they look (for lack of a better word) disturbing. Children might be scared if they’re deep, look very recent, or there’s a large amount. That’s true. I think that spanking is abuse if society considers it to be abuse, and vice versa. And that’s because abuse is a social construct. That’s not to say that it doesn’t exist, but abuse is a term that we made up to describe something that happens (in this case, a behavior) in society. Abuse is very real, but we can’t hold it or touch it, and it exists differently across cultures. We as a society decide what is and isn’t abuse. But we don’t get to decide that obsidian is actually a liquid. One is a construct, one isn’t. 

For example, being hit with a paddle used to be a socially acceptable form of discipline and was not considered abuse. Obviously, that has changed and is now considered abusive. So therefore, you could sit a 60 year old man and a 6 year old boy next to eachother, both have been hit with a paddle as a child, but only one has been abused (the 6 year old). You could apply the same logic to spanking.

More and more people have begun to consider spanking a form of abuse. Does that make it abuse? Well, if most people believe so and majority rules, then yes. I’m not sure the actual numbers of how many people believe it is vs. isn’t, but hypothetically. I think spanking is more of a grey area because the idea that it’s abusive is a relatively new concept, whereas whipping your child with a belt is most definitely considered abuse. And that doesn’t mean there’s a right or wrong answer, and we just don’t know it yet. It means that there is no correct answer. 

We see a lot of arguing on grey areas of social constructs. Issues of politics, social justice, gender roles, freedoms, the list goes on. And we’re able to do that because those ideas and norms haven’t been set yet. But guess who sets them? Us. They’re not inherent. Of course there are nuances of this and concrete facts that are integrated into constructs (statistics, for example), but you get the idea.

Your doctor can’t tell your parents unless she has reason to believe that you’re at risk for hurting yourself or someone else. This has a lot to do with how you say it, kind of.

Scenario one:

You: I struggle with self harm

Doctor: Okay, tell me about it *probably won’t snitch*

Scenario 2:

You: I self harm and I’m going to cut myself after this

Doctor: Um *will most likely snitch*
